Risk Radar

Sedex · B2B SaaS / ESG

Bringing supply-chain risk analysis into a clearer, more connected product experience.

Timeframe

Apr 2024 – Sep 2024

Role

Product Designer, leading end-to-end design in a focused team, co-owning platform consistency, and shaping goals, scope and success measures.

Team

A small initiative with a Tech Lead, Solutions Architect and Front-End Developer.

Tools

Figma, UserTesting, Dovetail, Miro, Jira, Confluence, Google Analytics, Qualtrics, Hotjar, ThoughtSpot and Intercom.

Tags
Product designPersonal initiativeB2B SaaSData consumptionESG

01

Context & problem

What is Sedex?

A global leader in supply chain data exchange, empowering businesses to make responsible and ethical decisions by providing transparency into supplier networks.

*Environmental, Social and Governance

What is the problem?

Our old tool called Radar produced inherent risk analysis for companies, serving as a predictive tool to help large organisations prioritise who to assess. Radar lived in a separate platform and its design language was completely different from the rest of Sedex’s toolkit.

What about the dashboard?

As we upgraded the platform’s design language, we also needed to update the dashboard. Because different widgets would appear on it, the designers came together and designed widgets using the knowledge from their focused teams. The opportunity was to incorporate Radar into the new dashboard as well.

Is there a future scope?

Because I was the designer on the supply-chain project, I took the initiative to bring Radar in as a separate effort. I designed the hierarchical visualisation of trade relationships first, and Radar’s prioritisation patterns and users’ map interactions would help us understand whether a future map-based supply-chain view could work.

02

Research & discovery

What does Radar do?

The problem was first highlighted to our customer support department, with the majority of our major customers raising concerns about supplier-network transparency on the platform.

How does it work?

I joined a large workshop with field experts and the developers who built the old Radar to understand how it worked.

The platform uses an engine that understands patterns from risks uncovered by Sedex’s assessment tools and generates a risk prediction, known as inherent risk in the industry.

Is it worth investing time to change this tool?

This question was important so we could determine whether to shut the tool down, leave it as it was, or bring it into the new dashboard. After looking at the numbers, we decided it was worth assigning a small team, including myself, a Tech Lead, a Solutions Architect and a Front-End Developer, to connect Radar with the new dashboard.

3,964

Total active users

Recorded in one week.

4,783

Total sessions

Users returned to use the tool repeatedly.

67%

Trust rate

Most users trusted Radar, but not enough to feel fully confident.

What do users tell us?

At this stage, I conducted several user research sessions. Customers said they used Radar to prioritise assessment requests, but I observed significant usability issues. Further analysis showed that interpreting the data was time-consuming and difficult to grasp quickly.

Users wanted Radar to live in the same platform they used to assess suppliers and analyse assessment data.

Google Analytics

The data showed that users interacted with the map most on this page. The hierarchy and filters therefore became secondary to the map experience.

Who uses Radar?

Radar began as an internal tool for Sedex’s ESG consulting team and was later released to customers as a standalone product alongside the main platform. It is used by Ethical Trade Coordinators, Health & Safety Officers and similar roles at companies such as Tesco, M&S, Walmart and Unilever. In Product, we defined a vision to bring the Radar interface and experience into the new dashboard.

Representative image generated with ChatGPT.

03

Design process

What is the tool hierarchy?

I produced a flowchart to clarify the hierarchical site structure and define the features for the new Radar.

First, what will the dashboard look like?

We introduced a bi-weekly Design Day, where the design team co-created the new dashboard. With clear ownership of different tools, each designer defined the widgets linked to their area.

What will Radar look like?

Using an AI assistant linked to my AI notetaker, I distilled my research and created initial design concepts for Radar on the new dashboard.

Concept images generated with ChatGPT.

How do the prototypes perform?

After testing mid-fidelity wireframes, I prototyped the high-fidelity direction and tested it to validate what could become the final concept.

Moderated testing

All existing customers who participated said the new Radar would make their working lives easier.

Unmoderated testing

The dashboard widgets were self-explanatory, and users found the new Radar fast and easy to understand.
04

Final solution

What does Radar do?

Radar helps enterprise Trade Coordinators prioritise which suppliers to assess first. When suppliers register their sites on Sedex, they inherit baseline risk informed by assessments of similar suppliers. Sedex’s AI then analyses assessment data and predicts which suppliers most require attention, giving coordinators a clear, actionable view.

The experience in motion

A short walkthrough of the redesigned dashboard and Radar, showing how risk insights fit into the wider workspace.

New dashboard

A unified, lightweight overview of supply-chain health, with Radar integrated in the side navigation and a consistent visual language for seamless, at-a-glance insight.

New Radar

The core risk tools users rely on a world map, actionable Latest Risks widget and category breakdown, were refined for faster prioritisation and everyday decision-making.

05

Impact & outcomes

What did the new Radar and dashboard achieve?

These were the goals set between the small Radar team and the wider Design team.

15%

More active users on Radar

More customers started using Radar after it was integrated into the same platform.

22%

Earlier discovery of high-risk suppliers

Risks were identified sooner for quicker follow-up.

27%

Faster high-risk intervention

Flag-to-start delay improved from 36 hours to 26 hours; intervention within seven days increased from 68% to 85%.

19%

More actionable findings

More assessments surfaced genuine issues.

06

Reflections & learnings

What did I learn?

01

Leading without a PM

How to bridge business goals and user needs, frame the problem, and facilitate the team to co-define scope and success so we moved fast with shared clarity.

02

Small-team velocity

How to ship in short cycles with lightweight rituals, balancing speed and quality without creating delivery debt.

03

Coordinating designers at pace

How to set clear patterns, run focused critiques and unblock quickly so the dashboard stayed consistent while work progressed in parallel.

04

Enterprise-first thinking

How to prioritise high-signal KPIs, auditability and immediate actions that fit enterprise workflows, not just polished visuals.

05

From overview to action

How to connect a health overview to prioritised, in-context actions through Radar, reducing friction between spotting a risk and acting on it.

06

Explainability builds trust

How to embed model explainers, decision logs and a shared glossary so stakeholders understood why something was risky, increasing adoption.

07

Measure what matters

How to define and instrument practical outcomes, time to insight, throughput and hit rate, so we could learn, iterate and prove impact.

Thank you!

01

Context & problem

What is Sedex?

A global leader in supply chain data exchange, empowering businesses to make responsible and ethical decisions by providing transparency into supplier networks.

*Environmental, Social and Governance

What is the problem?

The legacy platform presented supplier relationships in a spreadsheet-like table and supported only three tiers. Enterprises could not easily trace deeper connections to understand risks further along their supply chains.

The limitation

The data model stopped at three tiers, leaving deeper supplier relationships out of view.

The goal

Support as many relationship tiers as needed, helping customers trace their networks through suppliers and sites towards raw materials.

Why is it complicated?

Enterprise supplier networks can include thousands of organisations, hundreds of sites per supplier, subsidiaries and branching relationships that extend in many directions.

What are the numbers?

The scale of the platform shaped every design decision, from how information was grouped to how the interface loaded and helped users find specific suppliers.

90,000+

Total members

A large community expecting a return on investment.

5,000+

Enterprise suppliers

Large customers manage risk data across thousands of suppliers.

100+

Sites per supplier

Members may need to navigate hundreds of sites.

1,000+

Monthly sign-ups

The network grows by more than a thousand members each month.

Can supply chains be fully transparent and still be easy to navigate, so users can manage their risks efficiently?
02

Research & discovery

How did we know there was a problem?

Customer Support reported that many major customers were dissatisfied with supplier-network transparency. An Intercom survey reinforced this, with supply chain transparency receiving 180 votes from 634 responses.

Intercom survey results

How can the platform help you more?

250200150100500
89
Faster SAQ process
180
Supply chain transparency
162
Faster site search
203
Faster platform loading

Total votes: 634

*SAQ means Self-Assessment Questionnaire.

What were my first steps?

I joined customer calls and ran research workshops early, so I could understand the problem directly from the people managing complex supplier networks.

What did I learn?

Large enterprises often manage more than five thousand suppliers. Their highest risks tend to sit in raw-material tiers, frequently more than three or five relationships away from the enterprise. Hierarchy was therefore essential for prioritising risk-reduction strategies.

Customer journeys

I mapped how enterprise customers managed links and supplier relationships. The journeys showed no effective way to direct immediate attention when supply chains changed.

Supplier journeys

Supplier journeys exposed inefficient site-visibility controls, while suppliers still wanted clear ownership over what data they shared.

How did everyone interact?

Combining both journey maps made it clear that the experience involved platform touchpoints and direct user-to-user interactions between customers and suppliers.

What were the business goals?

Leadership expected that greater supply-chain visibility would reveal suppliers that were not Sedex members, creating an important opportunity for membership growth alongside the customer value.

03

Team & collaboration

What were the team dynamics like?

I worked as the Product Designer alongside a Product Manager, Tech Lead and 8–10 developers. We shared early assumptions, technical constraints and opportunities before committing to a direction.

User-story workshops

I led workshops that exposed a critical usability gap, users had no search function to filter a large volume of relationship data quickly.

Feasibility workshops

The Product Manager and Tech Lead confirmed that the platform relied on older technology and needed substantial data and service remodelling.

How did the design team respond?

The back-end work created time to improve the current interface. Together with the other designers and front-end developers, I helped establish a cleaner platform style that solved immediate usability problems while the data foundations were rebuilt.

File reorganisation

Under the Head of Product Design, we introduced a clearer page structure and UX notes to make design files easier to understand and hand over.

Tokenised design system

I coached the team in design tokens and updated the system with atomic components, improving communication and implementation with front-end developers.

How did this affect the process?

The shared foundations reduced legacy work and made the platform more scalable.

89

Updated components

Legacy components were removed from Storybook.

12

Updated design files

Figma files moved to the new structure.

20%

Faster development

More front-end tickets completed per sprint.

10%

Cheaper production

UI updates became more efficient and reusable.

04

Iteration & delivery

How did users react to changes?

I introduced improvements without disrupting the daily work of existing customers, while making the experience easier for new members to learn.

Google Analytics

With the Product Analyst, I set up event tracking and found that users relied heavily on the new search function.

Hotjar patterns

Behaviour recordings showed that nudges directed users to urgent tasks and the wider table improved information scanning.

Moderated testing

Existing customers valued the wider table and easier information consumption, but still needed deeper supply-chain transparency.

Unmoderated testing

New users could find a site through search, but could not confidently understand the trading hierarchy it belonged to.

What did not go well?

The data still contained duplicate relationships, loading remained slow and the product supported only three tiers.

150+

Duplicate links

ThoughtSpot highlighted unhealthy relationship data.

10+

Seconds loading

The existing data-fetching services were too slow.

3

Supported tiers

The core transparency limitation remained.

If AI identifies duplicate links and users are prompted to check them, users can clean unhealthy data before it affects the network.
If the interface is clear and fast, users are less likely to create the same relationships more than once.

What did the developers think?

As the back-end team rebuilt the repositories and services, I worked with them to identify front-end concepts that could surface hierarchical data quickly and expose discrepancies.

What was the happy path?

Users should arrive on the page, see urgent actions, drill into tiers, find a supplier or site and continue to the detailed data they need.

05

Solution explorations

What did we want to achieve?

Users needed to visualise their entire supplier network as a genuine hierarchy, then trace products back through the relationships to their raw materials.

What were the ideas?

We explored keeping the familiar data-table model with clearer tier tags, introducing a family-tree-style hierarchy, and using a linear transport-map concept to show product traceability.

How did I test the concepts?

I prototyped three major ideas and tested them through live conference research, collaborative workshops and unmoderated UserTesting studies.

What were the results?

The tree view and linear map tied as the strongest concepts. The table worked for individual sites, the tree communicated scale and hierarchy, and the linear view made pathways easy to follow.

Concept testing results

Votes from 80 participants.

403020100
8
Supply chain topsheet
36
Tree view
36
Linear view

Useful for viewing sites, but not the whole supply chain.

Strong hierarchy, with questions about very large networks.

Clear and calm, but less effective at showing scale.

Total votes: 80

Could the winning concepts work together?

Supplier networks communicate the full scale of trading relationships, supply chains group meaningful sections and pathways show the linear journey of a product.

If users can switch between the supplier network and the pathway, they can understand the supply chain both in bulk and in detail.

Proof of concept

We used Material UI tree components to test how quickly the new APIs could render nested relationships inside a data grid.

Linear pathway proof of concept

Because the design system already included a stepper and the page used caching, we could build and test a transport-map-style pathway quickly.

Performance

The rebuilt services and interface concepts fetched and rendered complex hierarchy data successfully in both internal and user testing.

User experience

The tree list became the best compromise, giving users clear hierarchical depth while remaining practical to build, scan and expand.

06

Final concept

What is the final concept?

A user lands on the supply-chain page and sees the complete supplier network in a data table with an expandable tree list. The hierarchy keeps complex relationships tidy while allowing the user to open as many tiers as needed, find a company and continue to its sites.

On the sites page, users can consume detailed site data and switch between tiers to trace all sites related to a product pathway.

07

Impact & outcomes

Impact for the business

The final platform exceeded the original visibility target and revealed suppliers that had not previously been assessed or identified as members.

8+

Supply-chain tiers supported

The new experience achieved the transparency goal.

1,000+

New suppliers discovered

Previously unassessed suppliers became visible.

Major user and product impact

I defined additional measures to understand how the experience improved customers’ return on investment and contributed to Sedex’s success.

30%

Faster data management

Measured through Google Analytics events.

40%

Fewer duplicate links

ThoughtSpot showed healthier relationship data.

15%

Higher retention

Measured through comparative Salesforce analytics.

25%

Better satisfaction

Measured through Tableau and Intercom surveys.

Other impact

Users reported greater efficiency when managing supplier relationships, stronger trust in the clearer hierarchy and more confidence assessing risk. The work also encouraged design consistency across multiple Sedex teams and touchpoints.

08

Reflections & learnings

01

Coaching

I helped the design team adopt semantic tokens, atomic components and stronger Figma practices, while also mentoring a Junior Product Designer.

02

Motivating the team

I made progress visible through frequent demos, short check-ins and weekly targets when long technical work reduced momentum.

03

Fast delivery

Frequent releases taught me to break large epics into smaller improvements that could scale over time.

04

Being proactive

I created learning content, introduced a weekly design critique and advocated for tokens and atomic design with developers.

05

Business presentations

I presented progress to executives and shared updates during global company meetings with more than 300 attendees.

06

Face-to-face research

At a Sedex conference, I recruited participants and ran live research on the three shortlisted concepts.

07

Exposure to development

Working closely with engineering increased my confidence with Kafka, Kotlin, JavaScript, HTML, monorepos and Storybook.

Thank you!

01

Context & opportunity

What is bnbme?

bnbme is an online booking service for short-stay and holiday homes, focused on premium travel experiences in the Middle East.

Dubai

The company began in Dubai, serving travellers looking for high-end stays and professionally managed properties.

Riyadh

Riyadh was the next expansion market, extending the premium offering to another major destination in the region.

What were the problems?

01

The discovery experience had received little design attention.

02

The third-party booking flow could not support bnbme add-ons.

03

Hosts had no in-house room-management platform.

The previous experience moved travellers between disconnected pages and a third-party booking flow, while the host-acquisition journey sat separately from the core product.

What was the goal?

Redesign the traveller journey, the hosts’ landing page and the management tools from scratch, using a mobile-first approach that could also support Arabic.

My design challenges

  1. 01

    Improve conversion across the full website.

  2. 02

    Design the Property Management System alongside the consumer experience.

  3. 03

    Keep the product mobile-first while supporting Arabic users.

02

Research & discovery

What did the owner want to achieve?

I ran vision workshops with the owner, Chief Commercial Officer, Lead Product Manager and Tech Lead to agree priorities and create a shared product direction.

Google Analytics

Analytics showed that the main journeys were not converting website traffic into completed bookings.

SurveyMonkey

A 26-person survey and customer reviews showed low trust, with visitors worried about scams and struggling to find room amenities.

What did the hosts say?

I ran research workshops with hosts listed on bnbme and competing platforms. Otter.ai captured the conversations and ChatGPT helped organise the findings.

Important figures

24,875

Landing-page views

Recorded over three months.

100%

Booking drop-off

No bookings were completed through the existing website.

$3,004

Annual external PMS cost

The yearly platform fee paid by bnbme.

The hypotheses

A familiar booking experience would make visitors feel more confident using bnbme.
Bringing room management in-house would reduce fees and encourage more hosts to list properties.

Who are we designing for?

Four personas helped balance the needs of travellers from Europe and the United States, travellers from Arabic countries, and property hosts.

What is the product vision?

A product-vision workshop aligned the team around a clear roadmap. I used ChatGPT for story mapping and early visual inspiration.

03

Finding a room

What did we tackle first?

The first release focused on the landing page, search results and room details, the earliest touchpoints in the customer journey and the pages already owned by bnbme.

How would a user search for a room?

I mapped the end-to-end search flow to understand where visitors needed reassurance, clearer filtering and stronger property information.

What direction should the interface take?

I explored an Airbnb-style discovery experience, a Booking.com-style information-rich experience, and a hybrid that combined both strengths.

What did 50 testers prefer?

UserTesting experiment results

Preference across three interface directions.

3020100
11
Booking.com style
12
Airbnb style
27
Hybrid style

Users valued the detailed hero, nearby content and destination sections.

The map-led discovery and cleaner room details were preferred.

The combined direction balanced cleanliness with enough detail.

Total testers: 50

Rebranding for trust

The new foundations retained gold as a luxury cue and introduced an Inter type scale that could work consistently in English and Arabic.

Final discovery experience

The landing page, search results and room details were finalised and handed over before the team moved to the booking journey.

04

Booking a room

UserTesting

People found rooms easily, but the third-party booking journey felt disconnected and the add-ons felt forced.

SurveyMonkey

Visitors liked the new discovery experience, but the limited room variety showed that more hosts also needed to be onboarded.

What companies have strong upselling journeys?

Airline booking flows provided the clearest precedent. Ryanair combined familiar progression, optional extras and clear skip actions better than more visually restrained airline experiences.

The revised flow

The booking journey used optional add-on steps, visible Skip and Next actions, and a clear progress tracker. This preserved momentum while still creating opportunities to upsell relevant services.

Mobile version

Testing confirmed that the anchored actions kept the experience clear without interrupting booking momentum.

Desktop version

The desktop interface felt trustworthy and gave the team confidence that the new journey could improve conversion.

05

Host tools & operations

How do we onboard more hosts?

The host journey needed to make the commercial value obvious, reduce the cost of managing rooms and keep sales contact points easy to reach.

Current external PMS

Beds24 had a good reputation, but it cost bnbme $3,004 each year and hosts paid an additional monthly fee for every listed room.

Cost analysis

The long-term investment showed that an in-house PMS could strengthen growth, improve reputation and remove recurring costs for hosts.

What would the dashboard look like?

Workshops with existing hosts and research into other PMS tools shaped an initial concept for the host dashboard.

What does the final product look like?

The final platform focused on the features hosts would use most often, including latest bookings, calendars, messaging, incoming requests and performance highlights. Additional details remain under a disclosure agreement.

Reflections & learnings

Leadership

Working as the only designer required clear prioritisation, confident decision-making and ownership of the complete process.

Design operations

Breaking the transformation into discovery, booking and host-management releases helped the team deliver value progressively.

Design system foundations

What components did I introduce?

Tabs

A reusable navigation pattern for switching between related content and workflows.

Notifications

A consistent pattern for communicating status, warnings and system feedback.

Dialogs

Dialog patterns that helped teams present focused decisions without losing context.

Graphs

Reusable data-visualisation components for complex enterprise reporting interfaces.

Panels

A flexible surface for controls, information and supporting actions across products.

Inputs

Sidebar

How do I design?

I adapt my process to each product and team, moving from deep understanding to evidence-backed delivery.

01

Understand and frame

I map the full journey, experience the product from the user’s perspective and work with users and colleagues to clarify the problem, goals, constraints and available resources.

02

Explore and refine

I compare multiple directions, using rapid prototyping and AI-assisted ideation before refining the strongest option around feasibility and timelines.

03

Test and align

I validate ideas with users, consult developers and use evidence to balance user needs, technical realities and business goals.

Accessibility statement

Designing for access is part of designing well.

I believe digital products should be usable by as many people as possible, regardless of ability, technology or circumstance. Accessibility is not an extra layer I add at the end of a project; it is part of how I understand and practise user experience design.

My personal commitment

As a neurodivergent person myself, accessibility is also personal to me. People perceive, process and interact with information in different ways, and those differences can change whether a product feels clear and empowering or unnecessarily difficult to use.

That perspective has made me increasingly conscious of designing beyond an assumed “average” user. I try to consider different ways of seeing, understanding, navigating and interacting with an interface from the beginning of the design process.

Accessibility of this website

I have designed and tested this portfolio with accessibility in mind, with the aim of meeting WCAG 2.2 Level AA wherever possible. My reviews include keyboard navigation, visible focus states, colour contrast, text readability, semantic structure, meaningful alternative text, responsive layouts, browser zoom and reduced-motion preferences.

For US-facing digital experiences, I also consider accessibility obligations under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), using WCAG as the practical benchmark for evaluating and improving web accessibility.

I do not consider accessibility a one-off checklist or describe a digital experience as permanently “100% accessible”. Products change, standards evolve and real users can uncover barriers that automated checks or design reviews miss. I therefore treat accessibility as an ongoing process of testing, learning and improving.

How this website was tested

This website has been reviewed using a combination of automated tools, manual checks, assistive technology and accessibility-focused user testing.

I have used tools including Google Lighthouse, Colour Contrast Analyser (CCA), HeadingsMap and Apple VoiceOver to assess areas such as automated accessibility issues, colour contrast, semantic structure, heading hierarchy, keyboard navigation and screen-reader behaviour.

I have also run structured user-testing sessions designed to work systematically through the relevant WCAG 2.1 and WCAG 2.2 success criteria, including Level AA criteria, alongside relevant ADA accessibility expectations. Guidance and testing resources from Level Access helped me structure these sessions and review the experience beyond what automated checks alone can identify.

Where issues were identified, I reviewed and updated the experience before testing again. Accessibility testing is an ongoing process, so I intend to continue reviewing this website as its content and functionality evolve.

My accessibility journey

My understanding of accessibility has developed throughout my career through hands-on product work, training, workshops and collaboration with specialists rather than through a single course or certification.

MUST Store

My first professional exposure came while designing mobile experiences for MUST Store, an e-commerce website. Working closely with the web developer gave me practical accessibility training and helped me understand how design decisions translate into the interfaces people actually navigate and use.

adam&eveDDB

While designing native mobile experiences at adam&eveDDB, including work intended to support local communities, I received further guidance from the Design Director around visual accessibility. This strengthened my understanding of colour, contrast, hierarchy, readability and designing interfaces that remain understandable across different users and contexts.

Sedex

At Sedex, accessibility became a much more established part of my day-to-day product practice. I took part in extensive workshops led by accessibility experts and actively advocated for accessibility while designing complex B2B SaaS products and contributing to shared design-system patterns.

Working on data-heavy enterprise software reinforced the importance of semantic structure, keyboard interaction, clear focus states, accessible reusable components and presenting complex information without creating unnecessary cognitive or visual barriers.

KINTO Join and Toyota

Today, at KINTO Join, part of Toyota Financial Services, I am a member of the Accessibility Council. Alongside applying accessibility principles to the products I design, I advocate for accessible design practices and help bring WCAG and US ADA considerations into wider conversations across the Toyota organisation.

Accessibility in my design practice

For me, accessibility is not a separate specialism sitting beside UX. It influences decisions about information hierarchy, interaction patterns, colour, typography, language, component behaviour, forms, navigation, errors, motion and how complex information is communicated.

It also means recognising the limits of automated testing. Tools are useful for identifying certain issues, but they cannot replace manual testing, human judgement or learning directly from people who experience accessibility barriers.

My commitment is to consider accessibility deliberately, advocate for it when decisions are being made, test the experiences I create, learn from people with different needs and improve the product when barriers are identified.

Feedback

Despite the testing and care I put into this website, there may still be areas I can improve. If you experience an accessibility barrier while using my portfolio, or notice something I could make more inclusive, I would genuinely appreciate hearing from you.
